topic: Bridging HL7 to FHIR Kills Real-Time Telemetry
postText:
Bedside monitors emit vitals every 500ms over raw HL7 v2 via plain MLLP (Minimum Lower Layer Protocol). No TLS. Plain TCP. Pipe delimited strings.

In modern healthcare IT, management wants that data normalized into standard FHIR Observation resources for analytics and cross-system interoperability. So engineers build synchronous microservices: read MLLP socket, parse pipe segments, validate against FHIR schema, invoke REST API.

Then ICU adds 40 beds. Ingestion dies.

HL7 v2 is dirt-cheap to emit, but FHIR JSON validation is CPU heavy. Synchronous REST writes introduce TCP handshakes and JSON serialization tax. Latency stacks up. Socket buffers fill, bedside monitors drop connections, and critical telemetry disappears from clinical dashboards.

Even worse: raw MLLP lacks native encryption. Running it across standard hospital VLANs without boundary controls risks exposing PHI/PII.

The fix requires decoupling ingestion from transformation:
1. Deploy lightweight edge gateways near bedside networks to terminate raw MLLP and wrap data inside mTLS tunnels.
2. Ingest raw payloads directly into an append-only message broker (Kafka/Redpanda) without parsing.
3. Run background worker pools to batch vitals into composite FHIR bundles asynchronously.

Keep hot ingestion paths lean. Data safety at bedside admits zero latency.

How does your team handle high-throughput bedside telemetry bridging without degrading core EHR responsiveness?
